title: Everest Base Camp Trek Difficulty and Altitude Explained
meta_description: How hard is the Everest Base Camp trek: walking hours, height gain, altitude profile from Lukla to Kala Patthar, rest days, AMS signs and training.
summary: The Everest Base Camp trek is challenging but not technical: 5–8 hours of walking a day on rocky trails, height gains of up to 800 m, and nights rising from 2,610 m at Phakding to 5,164 m at Gorak Shep. Altitude, not distance, is what makes it hard, so two acclimatisation days and a slow pace matter more than fitness.

sections.heading: How hard is it, honestly
paras: We grade the standard base camp trek as Challenging. There are no ropes, no climbing and no glacier crossings on the main route: the trail is a well-used path of stone steps, dirt, moraine and suspension bridges, and you sleep in a lodge every night. A porter carries your main bag, so you walk with a daypack of 5–7 kg.

What makes it hard is the combination of long days, steady climbing and thin air. The round trip from Lukla is about 130 km over 11 days of walking. Above 4,000 m there is roughly 40 percent less oxygen in each breath than at sea level, so a slope that takes 20 minutes at home takes 40 minutes at Lobuche. The cold, dry air at night and broken sleep add to the fatigue.

People who walk regularly, can hike 6 hours with a pack and arrive willing to go slowly usually reach base camp. The people who struggle are often the fittest, because they walk too fast in the first few days.

sections.heading: The altitude profile, day by day
paras: This is the profile of our 12-day trek, which follows the classic rule of sleeping no more than 300–500 m higher each night above 3,000 m, with a rest day for every 1,000 m or so of gain. Walking times are for an average group at a steady pace, including short breaks.

sections.heading: The four hardest days
paras: Day 2 to Namche is the first test: an easy riverside morning, then a steep climb of about 600 m from the Hillary Bridge to Namche in 2–3 hours, much of it on dusty switchbacks shared with yak trains. Day 4 to Tengboche drops to the Dudh Koshi at Phunki Tenga and climbs about 600 m through forest to the monastery, often in afternoon cloud.

Day 8 is the longest high day. You walk from Lobuche over the moraine to Gorak Shep in 2–3 hours, eat lunch, then walk another 2–3 hours each way to base camp on rough glacial rubble, sleeping at 5,164 m. Day 9 starts at about 4:30 am with a 2–3 hour climb up Kala Patthar in the dark and cold to 5,644 m, the highest point of the trek, followed by a long descent to Pheriche. Most trekkers say these two days are the hardest of their lives, and the most rewarding.

sections.heading: Altitude sickness: signs and rules
paras: Acute mountain sickness (AMS) affects many people above 3,000 m to some degree. Mild AMS feels like a hangover: headache, poor appetite, nausea, tiredness and poor sleep. It usually settles with a rest day at the same altitude. Two rarer conditions are dangerous: high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE), fluid on the brain, and high-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE), fluid in the lungs. Both can kill within hours and both are treated first by going down.

Our guides check each trekker's oxygen saturation and pulse with an oximeter every morning and evening above Namche, and ask simple questions about headache, appetite and sleep. These are the rules we follow on every trek:
list: Never go higher with symptoms of AMS; rest at the same altitude until they clear
Go down at once with any sign of HACE or HAPE: confusion, stumbling, breathlessness at rest, a wet cough or blue lips
Drink 3–4 litres of water a day and eat well, even without appetite
Avoid alcohol and sleeping pills above Namche
Ask your own doctor about acetazolamide (Diamox) before the trip; it helps acclimatisation but does not replace it
Tell your guide about any symptom, however small; hiding a headache is the most common mistake

sections.heading: Why the rest days matter
paras: The two acclimatisation days at Namche and Dingboche are not days off. Each one follows the principle of climb high, sleep low. At Namche you hike up to about 3,880 m at Hotel Everest View or Khumjung and come back down to sleep at 3,440 m. At Dingboche you climb part of the way up Nangkartshang Peak, towards 5,000 m, and sleep at 4,410 m. That extra height in the day, followed by a lower night, prompts the body to make more red blood cells and adjust its breathing.

Itineraries that skip one of these days to save time push the body faster than most people can adapt. Our 14-day trek adds a further buffer day, which we recommend for anyone over 55, anyone who has had AMS before and families travelling with teenagers.

sections.heading: Cold, dust and the Khumbu cough
paras: Altitude is the main challenge, but three smaller things wear people down on the way up. The first is cold. Above Dingboche the lodge bedrooms are unheated and often below freezing by morning, so sleep is broken unless your sleeping bag is rated to at least −15 °C in autumn and −20 °C in winter. A hot water bottle filled at dinner makes a large difference.

The second is the dry, dusty air. Yak trains and thousands of boots grind the trail into fine dust, and the cold air above 4,000 m holds almost no moisture. Many trekkers develop the Khumbu cough, a dry, persistent cough that can last for weeks after the trek. A buff or light mask over the mouth on dusty sections, throat lozenges and steady drinking all help.

The third is the downhill. The descent from Kala Patthar to Pheriche and then to Namche and Lukla covers about 2,800 m of height loss in three days, which is hard on knees. Trekking poles, strong quadriceps from training and a slower pace on the steep sections below Namche protect your joints.

sections.heading: Training and who should think twice
paras: Start training 8–10 weeks before departure. The goal is not speed but endurance on hills: walk for 4–6 hours with a 6 kg daypack at least once a week, use stairs or a steep treadmill for 45–60 minutes three times a week, and add leg strength work such as squats and step-ups to protect your knees on the descent. Break in your boots on these walks, not on the trail.

The trek is not suitable for everyone. People with heart disease, poorly controlled blood pressure, significant lung disease or recent surgery should talk to a doctor before booking, and many will be better served by the Everest View trek, which stays below 4,000 m, or by a helicopter tour. Children under about 12 can find the high days very hard, and pregnant women are generally advised not to trek to these altitudes.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Everest Base Camp trek for beginners?
faqs.a: It is a challenging trek but a beginner with good fitness can do it. There is no technical climbing, a porter carries your bag and you sleep in lodges. The difficulty comes from 5–8 hour days, steep climbs and altitude above 4,000 m. Train for 8–10 weeks with long uphill walks and choose an itinerary with two acclimatisation days.

faqs.q: How many hours a day do you walk on the Everest Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: Usually 5–6 hours, including breaks. The shortest day is the first, 3–4 hours from Lukla to Phakding. The longest are the base camp day, 7–8 hours from Lobuche to base camp and back to Gorak Shep, and the Kala Patthar day, 7–8 hours including the descent to Pheriche. Acclimatisation days have 3–5 hour hikes.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: The south-side Everest Base Camp in Nepal is at about 5,364 m on the Khumbu Glacier. You sleep below it at Gorak Shep, 5,164 m, and the highest point of the trek is Kala Patthar at 5,644 m. Lukla, where the trek starts, is at 2,860 m and Namche Bazaar at 3,440 m.

faqs.q: Will I get altitude sickness on the Everest Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: Many trekkers feel mild symptoms such as headache, poor sleep or loss of appetite above about 3,500 m, and these usually pass with rest. Serious altitude sickness is less common but possible. Walking slowly, drinking plenty, avoiding alcohol and taking both acclimatisation days greatly reduce the risk. Never climb higher with symptoms.

faqs.q: Should I take Diamox for Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: Acetazolamide, sold as Diamox, can help the body acclimatise and many trekkers carry it, but it is a prescription medicine with side effects and is not suitable for everyone, for example people with sulfa allergies. Ask your own doctor before the trip. It does not replace a slow ascent or rest days, and it does not mask serious symptoms.

faqs.q: Can a 60-year-old do the Everest Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: Yes, many people in their sixties reach base camp each season. What matters is health and preparation rather than age. Get a medical check-up, train for at least ten weeks and choose our 14-day itinerary for the extra buffer day. If you have heart or lung problems, consider the Everest View trek or a helicopter tour instead.

faqs.q: Is Kala Patthar harder than Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: Kala Patthar is steeper and higher, at 5,644 m against about 5,364 m, and it is climbed in the dark and cold before sunrise, so most trekkers find it harder. The walk to base camp is longer but flatter, over glacial moraine. If you feel unwell at Gorak Shep, skip Kala Patthar and start down.

faqs.q: How much height do you gain each day?
faqs.a: On our 12-day itinerary the biggest daily gains are Phakding to Namche, about 830 m, and Tengboche to Dingboche, about 540 m. Above Namche we keep sleeping gains to roughly 400–550 m a day, with rest days at Namche and Dingboche. On the base camp day you gain about 220 m to Gorak Shep, then 200 m more to base camp and back.

faqs.q: What fitness level do I need for Everest Base Camp?
faqs.a: You should be able to walk 6 hours on hilly ground with a light daypack and do it again the next day. A good test is climbing 1,000 m of stairs or hills in about 2–3 hours without being exhausted. Build to that over 8–10 weeks with weekly long hikes, regular stair sessions and leg strength exercises.
